opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about a lot, because the choice of baseliners really shapes what the number means. The time horizon is defined as the length of tasks, measured by how long they take humans, that a model can complete with some probability, say 50%. So "how long they take humans" is doing a lot of work, and which humans you pick matters.

The way I think about it, you want people who are genuinely skilled in the relevant domain: experienced software engineers, ML researchers, security people for the cyber tasks. You don't want novices, because then you're partly measuring how long it takes someone to learn the basics, and that inflates task lengths in a way that isn't very meaningful. But there's a subtlety. Our baseliners are typically experts in the general area who are new to the specific codebase or environment. They don't have the context that someone who's worked on a project for months would have. We've seen that people with deep context can be several times faster on the same task. So our numbers are best read as "how long it takes a competent professional without prior context," which is arguably the right comparison for a model dropped into a fresh environment, but it's not the same as "how long it takes the person who'd actually do this at work."

Then there are practical questions. Do you take the time of everyone who attempts the task, or only successful attempts? We've mostly used successful runs, which has its own selection effects, since the people who fail are often the ones who would have taken longer. You also want enough baseliners per task to average out noise, because individual completion times vary a lot, and you want incentives that encourage people to work at a realistic pace rather than rushing or dawdling.

So if I were advising on it: pick people who represent the professional population whose labor you care about, be explicit about how much context they have, collect multiple baselines per task, and be transparent that the absolute numbers depend on these choices. In some ways the trend matters more than the level. If you're consistent about who you baseline, the doubling time is fairly robust even when the absolute horizon would shift by a factor of a few under a different baseliner pool.

r001.rationale: The response recommends baseliners who represent the relevant professional population, giving experienced software engineers, ML researchers, and security professionals as examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and I think it's genuinely one of the harder methodological questions with the time horizon metric, because the whole thing is defined relative to humans. The metric is basically "how long would it take a human to do the tasks that the model can do with, say, fifty percent reliability," and so the choice of which humans you're talking about changes the number quite a bit.

The way we've approached it so far is that we try to use people who have relevant expertise for the task. So for the software engineering and ML research tasks, that means people who are professional software engineers or ML researchers, people who could plausibly be hired to do this kind of work. The baseliners aren't random people off the street, but they're also not the single best person in the world at that specific task. The thing we're trying to approximate is something like a competent professional who has the general skills needed, but who is encountering this particular task fresh.

And I think "fresh" is an important qualifier. One of the things that makes this hard is that the time it takes a human depends enormously on context. If you've been working in a codebase for six months, you can do a task in twenty minutes that might take someone new to the codebase four hours. The models are, in some sense, always coming in fresh, so there's an argument that the fair comparison is to humans who are also coming in fresh. But that also means our time horizons might overstate how impressive the models are relative to what a real employee who knows the codebase would do.

There are a few things I'd want METR to be careful about, or things I think we should keep improving on. One is that the baseliners we get are going to be a somewhat self-selected population. People who are willing to sit down and do a bunch of timed, somewhat artificial tasks for a research org are not a perfectly representative sample of the profession. We try to screen for people who are actually strong, but there's variance, and some baseliners will just be having a bad day, or get stuck on some environment issue that's not really about the task.

Another is that for a lot of the longer tasks, we have very few baseline data points. If a task takes eight hours, you can't get thirty people to do it. You might get two or three. So the human time estimates for exactly the tasks that matter most for the frontier of the metric are the noisiest ones. I think the honest thing to say is that the human times on the long tail are more like informed estimates than precise measurements, and we should be upfront about that uncertainty.

In terms of what I'd ideally want, I think the right target population is something like "the kind of person a company would actually hire to do this work," because the ultimate question people care about is whether these systems can substitute for or augment real workers. If you benchmark against world experts, you'll get a conservative number, and if you benchmark against novices, you'll get an inflated number, and neither of those really tells you what you want to know about economic or safety-relevant impact. So I'd lean towards experienced practitioners, with as much transparency as possible about who they are, how they were recruited, and how much variance there is in their times.

And I'd also say that no single choice is going to be right for every purpose. If you care about the question of whether a model could do dangerous autonomous research, maybe you want the comparison to be to strong researchers. If you care about labor displacement, you might want a broader slice. I think it's fine to pick one for the headline metric, but it would be good for us and for other people doing this kind of work to report sensitivity to the choice, so people can see how much the number moves if you change your assumptions about who the humans are.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using people a company would actually hire for the work, describing them as experienced practitioners with relevant professional expertise.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what you want the metric to tell you. If you want it to tell you when an AI system can substitute for a professional doing some piece of work, then you want the human baseline to be people who actually do that kind of work, with the relevant experience and context. Someone can be a very good software engineer and still be quite slow on a task in an unfamiliar codebase.

And I’d distinguish selecting people from selecting tasks. You could have very representative people, but if you give them tasks that are unusually easy to specify and evaluate, you’re still measuring a particular slice of their work.

So my preference would be to define the population you’re trying to make claims about, sample people from that population, and get multiple measurements where that’s practical. Then show how sensitive the time horizon is to the human baseline. If one person takes an hour and another takes four hours, that’s relevant uncertainty in what you mean by a four-hour task.

There’s also a reasonable case for keeping a fixed baseline so you can track progress over time. But I’d be careful about moving from ‘models are improving on this benchmark’ to ‘models can now do this many hours of a typical person’s work.’ The second claim needs a lot more justification.

r001.rationale: The response says to use people who actually do that kind of work and have relevant experience and context, matching the real-world population naturally expected to perform the tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to be clear about what population you’re trying to measure against. There isn’t some intrinsic human completion time for a task. Something that takes an experienced software engineer twenty minutes might take me several hours, and that difference changes the horizon you report even if the model’s performance is exactly the same.

For the kinds of software tasks METR studies, I’d want people who have the relevant skills, who are reasonably familiar with the tools, and who are making a serious effort. You don’t want the baseline to be dominated by people learning the programming language as they go. But you also don’t want to pick the world’s best person for each individual task and implicitly compare the model to this composite superhuman.

Ideally, you’d have multiple people attempt at least a subset of the tasks, so you could see how much the result depends on who you recruited. And I’d report that uncertainty alongside the uncertainty about the model’s success rate. If you’re using the metric to track progress over time, keeping the human baseline consistent is especially important. If you’re using it to say something about which jobs could be automated, then you need a baseline that actually represents the people doing those jobs. Those are related goals, but they don’t necessarily call for exactly the same selection procedure.

r001.rationale: The response recommends relevant skills and tool familiarity, and says a job-automation baseline should represent people doing those jobs. It does not clearly state that METR should generally base task completion times on the people naturally expected to perform the tasks in the real world; it presents that as one goal-specific approach.
